title: Staying in California, reluctant to enter the studios
summary: Edison, who had visited California with Basie since 1940, was wary of studio work and learned from top studio trumpeters.

story.theme_name: Jazz musicians in the movies and film scoring
story.community_name: Studio work and jingles: New York session life

blocks.x: But then, '52, I stayed out here and I became -- well, I had been coming to California since 1940, you know, with

Count Basie. I knew a lot of musicians out here. And I became acquainted with Nelson Riddle and those were the days that I was reluctant to go in the studios because, you know, when you play studio music and play jazz music, it's a different ballgame, you know. Jazz, you're on your own when you're out there playing. And you're playing what you were born to do. The thing that you liked to do.
Right. And I knew that, you know, just like the fellows that I was going to play with, like they knew their horns because they had been trained to play in studios. So --
And, of course, they're all lightning readers.
OH, yes. Well, they were like Manny Klein, he's a fantastic blower, you know. The late Conrad Gozzo, the late Mickey Manzano, Conti Candoli, Steve --
Yeah, they were all -- Pete Candoli, they were all playing studio bands around here.
Was that Ray Linn in there?
Ray Linn was out here at the time. He was in the studio bands. Those guys were trained musicians, you know. They had been taking lessons on their horns when

my mother couldn't even afford to give me lessons, you know. But they were trained to do that and I owe a lot of my success in the studios -- I can attribute to those guys, the conversation and the experience that I had playing with them, and their knowledge that they gave me that was -- I think, my success in the studios was due to them. Because I knew --
They could tell you technical things.

Oh, yes. I wasn't equipped to do studio work. And there was no need for me to BS myself and be embarrassed, you know. My reading wasn't that fast. And, you know, when you're in the studios, you have one rehearsal and then you go to the chord, you know. You run it down a couple of times and then the dynamics and everything, the mistakes have been ironed out and you get ready to record. That's, you know, you have to be -- your eyesight has to be good, you have to watch direction, you have to blend with the other musicians. There's so much you have to learn.
And I knew I wasn't equipped with that knowledge so I used to ask, you know, and was humble, and I knew that when the light would go on that I would falter someplace.
Because you knew you could do it.
I could do it. Yeah, that's right. But I'd get there, sometimes, at a date, half hour before time. And
